Independent sources checked (DOE FEMP minimum-efficiency page, ENERGY STAR key product criteria, UMD Extension heat-pump page, OpenStax College Physics 2e section 15.5) define COP and HSPF separately but no single primary source states the seasonal identity verbatim with calibration range; defer to a dedicated seasonal-performance batch with HSPF Appendix M/M1 procedure scope.

gaps: All four records require vocabulary/dimension extensions: units W, J, kg, K, m, m2, W/(m*K), J/(kg*K), m2*K/W and quantities electrical_power, operating_duration, sensible_heat_transfer, temperature_difference, thermal_conductivity, heat_transfer_area, conduction_thickness, conductive_heat_transfer_rate, thermal_resistance_area_normalized. Current runtime only supports energy/currency units (1, percent, kWh, Wh, USD, USD/kWh).

Candidate quantity aliases for review: electrical_power vs future active/reactive power split; operating_duration is total active time across the declared interval, not continuous elapsed wall time including off periods; temperature_difference is a Kelvin/Celsius difference (offset-free), not an absolute temperature; thermal_resistance_area_normalized (R=L/k, m2*K/W) vs absolute thermal_resistance (R_th=L/(k*A), K/W) — only the former is curated here.

handoff.summary: Batch b01 curates 4 atomic building-energy thermal models: constant-power electricity consumption (kWh from W and h), sensible heat without phase change, steady 1D conductive rate through a plane slab, and area-normalized thermal resistance of one homogeneous layer. All are requires-extension (physical SI units outside current energy/currency runtime). Seasonal SPF/HSPF audit deferred with sources.

assumptions: source assumption: electrical power P is effectively constant over the declared operating interval (OpenStax E=Pt with P for time t; EIA one-Watt-for-one-hour definition).
application profile: t is total active operating time in hours within the interval (accumulated on-time); off-period consumption is treated as zero and is not inferred.
Same device/operating condition and the same energy boundary for P and E; device consumption does not by itself establish purchased grid electricity or tariff scope.

constants.locator: Eqs. 20.35-20.36: 60,000 W*h = 60.0 kW*h; EIA example 200 Wh = 0.2 kWh
constants.meaning: watts per kilowatt; converts watt-hours to kilowatt-hours

gaps: Requires vocabulary/dimension extensions: input quantity electrical_power in W, input quantity operating_duration in h, and power*time=energy dimensional rule. Current runtime has electricity_consumption in kWh but no power or hour quantities.
Candidate alias: electrical_power means constant active electrical input power of the device over the declared interval, not instantaneous peak or nameplate alone.

models.inverse_notes: E and positive t determine P = E*1000/t; E and positive P determine t = E*1000/P. Zero-duration guard excludes division by zero for P inversion; zero-power with zero-energy leaves duration underdetermined (any t satisfies 0=0). Substitution checked: E=60, t=1000 gives P=60*1000/1000=60 W. No negative-power branch; export/generation needs a separate signed model.
limitations: Excludes time-varying power (needs load profile or integral over P(t), not expressible in scalar v1).
Excludes losses outside the declared device boundary, standby/off consumption, and tariff/billing rules; energy quantity alone does not establish cost or grid scope.

references.method: Published result: OpenStax Eq. 20.35 reports E=(60 W)(1000 h)=60,000 W*h and Eq. 20.36 reports 60.0 kW*h. Arithmetic replay 60*1000/1000=60 exactly; no rounding beyond the reported one-decimal kWh.
references.provenance: Published textbook worked example converted from reported W*h to kWh by the source itself

references.method: Published result: EIA Measuring electricity states a 40-W (0.04 kW) bulb for five hours uses 200 Wh, i.e. 0.2 kWh. Arithmetic replay 40*5/1000=0.2 exactly.
references.provenance: Published agency example; reported Wh converted to kWh by the source (200 Wh = 0.2 kWh)

rejection_cases.reason: Negative constant power violates the nonnegative-consumption profile; generation/export requires a different signed model.
Operating duration t is required; power alone does not determine energy.

relationship.locator: Section 20.4, Eq. 20.34 (E=Pt) with Eqs. 20.35-20.36 unit step; EIA page sections 'Electricity is measured in Watts and kilowatts' and 'Electricity use over time is measured in Watthours' with 40-W 5-hour example
relationship.translation_notes: Source E=Pt is stated generally (P in watts, t in seconds gives joules; t in hours gives watt-hours). This record specializes units for building-energy accounting: P in W, t in h, E in kWh, so E(kWh)=P(W)*t(h)/1000. Pure literal 1000 is the exact W/kW prefix factor (NIST SP 811 prefix rule; OpenStax/EIA examples divide by 1000). Dimensional check: W*h = Wh (energy); Wh/(W/kW) = kWh (energy). No other substitution; constant-power scope retained from source.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: power is the rate of energy use so E=Pt (Eq. 20.34); the billing unit kWh is consistent with E=Pt; students can verify 1 kW*h=3.6e6 J; worked example computes (60 W)(1000 h)=60,000 W*h = 60.0 kW*h and cost at $0.12/kWh.

assumptions: source assumption: no phase change and no work done on or by the system; heat is proportional to mass and temperature change with material/phase-specific specific heat (OpenStax Sec. 14.2).

Specific heat c is treated as constant over the stated temperature interval for the given substance and phase; temperature dependence is negligible for this interval (source notes weak dependence except gases).
Same homogeneous substance sample, phase, and pressure/volume context for m, c, and dT; dT is the signed change Tf-Ti in K or C degrees (identical increments).

gaps: Requires vocabulary/dimension extensions: mass in kg, specific_heat_capacity in J/(kg*K), temperature_difference in K, sensible_heat_transfer in J, and energy=mass*specific_heat*temperature_difference rule.

Candidate aliases: sensible_heat_transfer is signed heat added (positive heating, negative cooling); temperature_difference is offset-free (K increments equal C-degree increments), not absolute temperature.

models.inverse_notes: Q with known m and c gives dT=Q/(m*c) (requires m>0, c>0); Q with known m and dT nonzero gives c=Q/(m*dT); Q with known c and dT nonzero gives m=Q/(c*dT). Zero dT with zero Q leaves partitioning underdetermined. Substitution checked: Q=62790, m=0.25, c=4186 gives dT=62790/(0.25*4186)=60 K. Algebraic inversion does not establish calorimetric invertibility when mixing or losses occur.
limitations: Excludes phase change (melting, freezing, vaporization) and any work exchange; latent heat needs a separate model (source Sec. 14.3).
Excludes temperature-dependent c(T) integration and gas c_v vs c_p distinction; use the stated constant-c interval only.

references.method: Published result with unit conversion: source Eq. 14.4 reports Qw=0.250*4186*60=62.8 kJ; expected stored as 62800 J. Arithmetic replay gives 62790 J (10 J below reported, from 62.8 kJ one-decimal rounding). Tolerance 60 J covers half output rounding unit (0.05 kJ=50 J) plus small input-rounding propagation.
references.provenance: Published textbook worked example (heating 0.250 L water 20 C to 80 C) converted from kJ to J

references.method: Published result with unit conversion: source Eq. 14.5 reports QAl=0.500*900*60=27.0 kJ; expected stored as 27000 J. Replay is exact at 27000 J. Tolerance 60 J covers half output rounding unit (0.05 kJ=50 J).
references.provenance: Published textbook worked example (0.500 kg aluminum pan, same 60 K rise) converted from kJ to J

rejection_cases.reason: Zero mass ceases to describe a substance sample; guard m>0 rejects it (not an admissible ideal boundary for this definition).
Specific heat c is required; mass and temperature change alone do not determine heat.

relationship.locator: Section 14.2, Eq. 14.2 (Q=mcDeltaT) with Eqs. 14.4-14.5 worked evaluation and Table 14.1 specific heats
relationship.original_equation: Q = mcDeltaT (Eq. 14.2), where Q is heat transfer, m mass, DeltaT temperature change, c specific heat; example Qw=mw*cw*DeltaT=0.250*4186*60.0=62.8 kJ
relationship.translation_notes: Symbol transcription only: source Q,m,c,DeltaT mapped to locals Q,m,c,dT (dT = Tf-Ti, same K/C increment). Units normalized to SI: m in kg, c in J/(kg*K), dT in K, Q in J. Dimensional check: kg * (J/(kg*K)) * K = J (energy). No hidden latent or work terms; scope sentence (no phase change, no work) retained in assumptions.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: assuming no phase change and no work, experiments show heat depends on temperature change, mass, and substance/phase; the quantitative relation is Q=mcDeltaT (Eq. 14.2) with c the heat to raise 1.00 kg by 1.00 C in J/(kg*K) or J/(kg*C) and identical K/C increments; worked example heats 0.250 kg water 60 C with 4186 J/(kg*C) to get 62.8 kJ and 0.500 kg aluminum with 900 to get 27.0 kJ.

assumptions: source assumption: steady one-dimensional conduction through a plane slab of uniform thickness with fixed face temperatures, constant area, and constant thermal conductivity; temperature varies linearly from hot to cold (Univ. Physics Sec. 1.6).
Same slab, material, area, thickness, and boundary-temperature pair for all quantities; lateral heat escape is negligible (source rods/slab are treated as insulated except at faces).
dT is the signed face-to-face difference Th-Tc (K increments); k is evaluated near the stated temperature (source Table 1.5 near 0 C).

gaps: Requires vocabulary/dimension extensions: thermal_conductivity in W/(m*K), heat_transfer_area in m2, conduction_thickness in m, temperature_difference in K, conductive_heat_transfer_rate in W, and power=conductivity*area*difference/thickness rule.
Candidate alias: conductive_heat_transfer_rate is the signed steady rate from hot to cold face; magnitude form with absolute dT is a qualified application profile, not a separate model.

models.inverse_notes: P with known k, A, L gives dT=P*L/(k*A) (requires k>0, A>0); P with known A, dT, L gives k=P*L/(A*dT) requiring nonzero A*dT; P with known k, dT, L gives A=P*L/(k*dT) requiring nonzero k*dT. Zero dT with zero P leaves geometry/conductivity underdetermined. Substitution checked: P=46.55, k=0.035, A=0.95, L=0.025 gives dT=46.55*0.025/(0.035*0.95)=35 K. Thickness zero is excluded (no slab); sign follows dT.
limitations: Excludes convection, radiation, thermal storage/transients, composite-series counter-examples beyond equal-area slabs, and temperature-dependent k; differential form P=-k*A*dT/dx is out of scalar-format scope.
Excludes edge effects, contact resistance, and moisture/airflow dependence; source conductivities are representative values near 0 C, not defaults for any climate or material lot.

references.method: Published result: Univ. Physics Sec. 1.6 icebox example computes P=(0.035)(0.950)(35)/0.0250=46.6 W and Q=P*t=4.03e6 J for one day. Replay gives 46.55 W; tolerance 0.1 W covers the reported one-decimal rounding (0.05 W) plus input rounding.
references.provenance: Published textbook worked example (polystyrene foam icebox, 35 K across 2.50 cm)

references.method: Published result: College Physics 2e Sec. 14.5 Eqs. 14.27-14.29 with k=0.010 J/s/m/C, same geometry and 35 C difference, reports Q/t=13.3 J/s. Replay gives 13.30 W exactly; tolerance 0.05 W covers one-decimal rounding.
references.provenance: Published textbook worked example (Styrofoam icebox, same geometry, lower conductivity table value) as materially different calibration

rejection_cases.reason: Zero thickness ceases to describe a slab (no material layer); guard L>0 rejects it rather than returning an infinite rate.
Thermal conductivity k is required; geometry and temperature difference alone do not determine the rate.

relationship.locator: Univ. Physics Sec. 1.6, Eq. 1.9 (P=kA(Th-Tc)/d) with icebox evaluation; College Physics 2e Sec. 14.5, Eq. 14.26 (Q/t=kA(T2-T1)/d) with Eqs. 14.27-14.29
relationship.translation_notes: Local L renames source d (thickness) to avoid confusion with differentials; local dT = Th-Tc = T2-T1 (same K/C increment). Local P = Q/t = dQ/dt (steady rate). Units normalized: k in W/(m*K), A in m2, dT in K, L in m, P in W. Dimensional check: (W/(m*K))*m2*K/m = W (power). Sign follows dT (hot-minus-cold positive in source magnitude convention).

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: the steady conductive rate through a slab is deduced from and confirmed by experiments as proportional to area, temperature difference, and conductivity and inversely proportional to thickness: P=kA(Th-Tc)/d (Eq. 1.9) with P in watts, A area, d thickness, Th-Tc difference, k conductivity; more generally P=-kA dT/dx with linear profile for constant P and A.

assumptions: source assumption: single homogeneous plane layer of uniform thickness with 1D steady conduction, constant conductivity, and equal face areas (Univ. Physics two-conductor method; R factors add for series layers).
Same layer, material, thickness interval, and conductivity reference temperature for L and k; faces are isothermal and lateral escape is negligible.
R is area-normalized (per unit area); absolute resistance R_th=R/A requires equal areas and is not separately curated here.

gaps: Requires vocabulary/dimension extensions: conduction_thickness in m, thermal_conductivity in W/(m*K), thermal_resistance_area_normalized in m2*K/W, and length/conductivity rule.
Distinguish from absolute thermal resistance R_th=L/(k*A) in K/W and from US customary R in ft2*F*h/Btu; only SI area-normalized R=L/k is curated. Conversion to IP R needs a separate adapter.

models.inverse_notes: R with known L gives k=L/R (requires R>0 implied by guards); R with known k gives L=R*k. Zero-thickness/no-layer and zero-conductivity (perfect insulator, infinite R) are excluded by guards and have no finite inverse. Substitution checked: R=0.00313, L=0.25 gives k=0.25/0.00313=79.87 W/(m*K) recovering steel table value 80 within rounding. Single-layer R adds in series only for equal areas; unequal areas need 3D treatment per source Significance note.
limitations: Applies only to one homogeneous plane layer under the stated 1D steady equal-area scope; composite U-factor assembly with convection/films needs additional series terms not curated here.
Excludes temperature/moisture-dependent k, contact resistance, and the still-used US IP R convention (ft2*F*h/Btu); do not substitute table k as a default for any climate or lot.

references.method: Published result: Univ. Physics two-conductor example reports Rsteel=3.13e-3 m2*C/W from L=0.25 m and k=80 W/m*C. Replay 0.25/80=0.003125 (5e-06 below reported). Tolerance 1e-05 covers reported 3-significant rounding (half unit 0.005e-3=5e-06) plus propagation.
references.provenance: Published textbook worked values (steel rod segment) as area-normalized resistance

references.method: Published result: same example reports RAl=1.14e-3 m2*C/W from L=0.25 m and k=220 W/m*C. Replay 0.25/220=0.0011364 (3.6e-06 below reported). Tolerance 1e-05 covers 3-significant rounding.
references.provenance: Published textbook worked values (aluminum rod segment, materially different conductivity) as second calibration

rejection_cases.reason: Zero conductivity would imply infinite resistance (perfect insulator limit), outside the finite-conductivity layer definition; guard k>0 rejects it.
Conductivity k is required; thickness alone does not determine resistance.

relationship.locator: Univ. Physics Sec. 1.6 two-conductor second Solution ('Recall that R=L/k. Now P=ADeltaT/R') with Rsteel/RAl evaluation and 'ratio d/k, called the R factor' prose; College Physics 2e Sec. 14.5 'ratio d/k is called the R factor' prose
relationship.original_equation: R = L/k; P = ADeltaT/R (or DeltaT = PR/A); R factor = d/k with rate inversely proportional to R
relationship.translation_notes: Derived definition from the slab rate: from P=k*A*dT/L, define area-normalized R=L/k so P=A*dT/R. Source states R=L/k explicitly and d/k as the R factor with inverse proportionality. Local L = source d/L thickness; local k = source k. Units: m / (W/(m*K)) = m2*K/W. C-degree/W vs K/W identical for differences. Dependency on the steady slab rate is identified rather than claimed verbatim as a standalone postulate.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: the second solution method recalls R=L/k and writes P=ADeltaT/R (DeltaT=PR/A), evaluates Rsteel=3.13e-3 and RAl=1.14e-3 m2*C/W for 0.25 m rods, adds R factors for series layers, and notes adding R values is common for insulated walls; earlier prose defines the ratio d/k as the R factor with rate inversely proportional to R.
